## Today's goal

Today we connect your laptop to GitHub, clone the private course repository that Amanda and I prepared for you, and send one commit back to GitHub.

# Your Course Repository

## Git, GitHub, GitHub CLI, and RStudio

These tools work together but have different jobs.

| Tool | Job |
|---|---|
| Git | records versions of files on your computer |
| GitHub | stores and shares a Git repository online |
| GitHub CLI (`gh`) | connects your computer to your GitHub account |
| RStudio | supplies buttons for common Git operations |

Your repository is named `course-YOUR-USERNAME`. Only you, Amanda, and I can see it.

Clean 01a, 01b, and 02a workbooks are included for reference. They don't contain your earlier answers; you don't need to redo them.

# Identify and Authenticate

## RStudio's Console and Terminal

RStudio contains two different places where you can type commands:

- The **Console** runs R code and usually begins each input line with `>`.
- The **Terminal** runs a system shell. We use it for programs such as Git and GitHub CLI.

RStudio displays the Terminal inside the IDE, but the commands still follow the rules of the shell it opened. The Terminal lets us ask the computer where we are, see which files are there, and run tools that do not have RStudio buttons.

## Linux: do nothing

RStudio opens a standard Linux shell. Leave the default Terminal setting in place. The commands in this lesson will work as shown, and paths use forward slashes, such as `/home/name/course-project`.

## Mac: do nothing

RStudio opens the Mac's default shell, normally `zsh`. Leave the default Terminal setting in place. The commands in this lesson will work as shown, and paths use forward slashes, such as `/Users/name/course-project`.

## Windows: choose Git Bash

Git Bash is supplied with Git for Windows. It provides the commands and path conventions used in this lesson while working with your Windows programs and files.

Choose **Tools → Global Options → Terminal**. Set **New terminals open with** to **Git Bash**, click **Apply**, and open a new Terminal. A Windows path such as `C:\Users\Name` appears as `/c/Users/Name` in Git Bash.

## Find where the Terminal starts

Run each line separately:

```bash
pwd
ls
```

`pwd` is short for **print working directory**. It prints the folder where the Terminal is currently working. Any command that reads or changes a file will begin from this location unless you give it another path.

`ls` is short for **list**. It prints the names of the files and folders in the working directory. Before cloning, you may see your home folder and personal files. The course folder doesn't exist on your laptop yet.

## Check the programs

In RStudio, open the **Terminal** tab, usually beside the Console. If it is not visible, choose **Tools → Terminal → New Terminal**. Run each line separately:

```bash
git --version
gh --version
```

`git` and `gh` name the programs. `--version` asks each one to identify itself. A version number means the program is available to RStudio's Terminal.

## Check Git's identity

```bash
git config --global user.name
git config --global user.email
```

`config` reads a Git setting. `--global` means the setting applies across your account on this laptop. The final part names the setting to read.

If both answers are correct, do not change them. Otherwise, replace the examples below and run only the line that needs correction:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

The quotation marks keep each value together. These settings identify your commits; they do not sign you into GitHub.

## Authenticate with GitHub CLI

Run:

```bash
gh auth login --web --git-protocol https --clipboard
```

- `gh auth login` begins GitHub authentication.
- `--web` uses GitHub's browser sign-in.
- `--git-protocol https` selects the connection used in this course.
- `--clipboard` copies the temporary sign-in code.

When the browser opens, paste the temporary code, confirm the correct GitHub account, and authorize GitHub CLI. Return to RStudio's Terminal and run these lines separately:

```bash
gh auth setup-git
gh auth status
```

`setup-git` tells Git to use GitHub CLI's stored credential when it contacts GitHub. `status` reports the recognized account without displaying the credential.

That's authentication finished. Next we'll clone once in the Terminal and open the project. After that, we'll use RStudio's Git buttons.

# Clone Once

## Clone in the Terminal

Cloning downloads the repository and its history to your laptop. After signing in, run this once, replacing `YOUR-USERNAME` with your GitHub username:

```bash
gh repo clone uh-pols6394-fall26/course-YOUR-USERNAME
```

`gh repo clone` downloads the repository. `uh-pols6394-fall26` is our organization; the slash separates it from your repository name. The new folder appears inside the Terminal's current directory.

Choose **File → Open Project**, enter the new `course-YOUR-USERNAME` folder, and open `pols6394.Rproj`.

## RStudio's clone route: watch only

Once `gh auth login` and `gh auth setup-git` are complete, RStudio can use that same authentication to clone a private repository.

I'll show **File → New Project → Version Control → Git**: paste the repository's HTTPS URL, choose a parent folder, and click **Create Project**. RStudio downloads the repository and opens the project.

**Don't do this now.** You've already cloned and opened your course repository. Repeating the clone would create a second copy, making it easy to edit the wrong one. Keep using the project you already opened.

For a future repository, the URL comes from its green **Code → Local → HTTPS** button. If RStudio asks for credentials, cancel and check `gh auth status` and `gh auth setup-git` in the Terminal. GitHub account passwords won't authenticate a clone.

Open RStudio's Terminal and run:

```bash
git status
```

Click **Pull** in RStudio's Git pane. The RStudio Terminal equivalent is:


`pull` downloads commits that are on GitHub but not yet on your laptop. Today it may report `Already up to date.`

## Render the workbook

1. Open `03a-workbook.qmd` in RStudio's Source pane and click **Save**.
2. Click **Render** at the top of the Source pane.
3. Wait for the HTML preview to open, then check that your notes appear.

Rendering creates `03a-workbook.html` beside the source file. Render again whenever you change the workbook; the existing HTML doesn't update itself. The HTML is ignored by Git, so you commit the `.qmd` source.

## Inspect before committing

Then inspect what changed:

```bash
git status
git diff
```

`git status` names changed files. `git diff` shows the changed lines that have not yet been staged. Confirm that `03a-workbook.qmd` is the file you intended to change.

## Commit with RStudio

1. Open the **Git** tab in the Environment–History–Git pane.
2. Check **Staged** beside `03a-workbook.qmd`.
3. Click **Commit**.
4. Enter `Complete Workbook 03a`.
5. Click **Commit**, then close the commit window.

At the top of the Git pane, you should see: **“Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 1 commit.”**

Your project has one saved commit that hasn't been sent to GitHub. `origin/main` is Git's record of the GitHub branch from the last synchronization. Click **Push** in the next step to send your commit; after a successful push, the “ahead” message should disappear.

The equivalent RStudio Terminal commands are shown here for reference:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Complete Workbook 03a"
```

`git add .` stages changes under the current project folder. `git commit` records the staged changes, `-m` says that the next value is the message, and the quotation marks keep the message together. Do not run these after making the same commit with RStudio.

Confirm the commit in RStudio's **History** window. You should see `Complete Workbook 03a`. Close History when you've checked it.

## Push to GitHub

Click **Push** in RStudio's Git pane. The RStudio Terminal equivalent is:

```bash
git push
```

`push` sends your local commits to your private repository on GitHub.

# See It on GitHub

## Inspect the shared copy

1. Return to your repository in the browser and refresh the page.
2. Find `Complete Workbook 03a` above the file list.
3. Click that commit message and inspect the changed file and highlighted lines.
4. Return to the repository and open `03a-workbook.qmd`.
5. Return once more and notice that GitHub displays `README.md` on the repository's front page.

This is the copy shared with Amanda and me. You can read files, inspect changes, and link to a specific commit without opening RStudio. The repository remains private.

# The Routine from Here

## How new lessons arrive

Amanda or I will add released files to your private repository on GitHub. At the start of class:

1. Open this existing RStudio project.
2. Click **Pull**, or run `git pull`.
3. Open the new workbook.

Do not clone the repository again. We will not replace workbooks from classes you have already completed.

## If something fails

Stop at the first error, leave RStudio's Terminal visible, and ask Amanda or me. Do not run guessed repair commands. The first error usually identifies the stage that failed.

- `command not found` means the program is unavailable to RStudio's Terminal.
- A username box appearing means the sign-in didn't take; check `gh auth status`.
- `authentication failed` means GitHub CLI is not connected to the expected account.
- `repository not found` points to the URL, invitation, or repository permission.
- `not a git repository` means RStudio's Terminal is in the wrong folder.
- `nothing to commit` means the file was not saved or did not change.

## Mini-project 2: recover an uncommitted edit

Begin only if `git status` reports a clean working tree.

1. Open `README.md`, add `TEMPORARY TEST — remove me` below its title, and save.
2. Find the modified `README.md` in the **Git** pane and click **Diff**.
3. Confirm that the diff shows only the temporary line.
4. Select `README.md` and choose the Git pane's **Revert** command. It may be under **More**.
5. Confirm the warning.
6. Check that the temporary line disappears and the Git pane is clean.

Revert discards an uncommitted edit. Here we use it only on a change made for this exercise.
